job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Top priorities for the markup:** (1) Sec. 7(a) and 7(b) conflict, so the prohibition may lapse on its own schedule. (2) Sec. 3(c) lets large-scale recovery continue under an undefined "environmental assessment" label. (3) The registry and reporting duties in Sec. 4 have no penalty. (4) Sec. 2(1)(A)'s "single vessel" language lets a fleet split production below the threshold. (5) Sec. 3(b) grandfathers an undefined "exploration license" with no limits.

**Definitions (Sec. 2)**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** "Single vessel" lets an operator split production across several vessels, each under 10,000 metric tons per year, and the bill has no affiliate or aggregation rule.
2. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The bill doesn't define how tonnage is measured (recovered vs. delivered or processed, wet vs. dry weight, nodules vs. sediment or overburden), so operators can argue about whether the threshold was crossed. Sec. 4 reports don't require a measurement method either.
3. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** "Other mineral resources" is undefined, so it's unclear whether the prohibition reaches sulfide deposits, cobalt crusts, or other non-nodule resources. Aligning with existing statutory definitions would help.
4. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** "From the seabed" and the 200-meter depth floor are undefined, and it's unclear whether recovery from the water column or activity in shallower water counts. The conjunctive test (tonnage and depth) also means falling just under either threshold takes an activity outside the definition.
5. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" is never defined in Sec. 2, and it's unclear whether it means the Commerce Secretary (NOAA) or the Interior Secretary, who oversees most offshore mineral leasing. Sec. 6 uses "Secretary of State," so the ambiguity is not just a drafting slip.
6. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** The "comparable risks" determination has no standard, process, notice, record requirement, deadline, or judicial review, so it can be contested or delayed. The bill also doesn't say whether an activity is lawful while a determination is pending.
7. **Sec. 2(2):** "U.S. person" covers only citizens and corporations organized under state law. It appears to exclude LLCs, partnerships, and federally chartered entities, even though LLCs and special-purpose vehicles are common in mining ventures. The District of Columbia and the territories are also not mentioned.
8. **Sec. 2(2) and 3(a):** The definition doesn't reach foreign-organized subsidiaries or affiliates controlled by U.S. companies, so a U.S. firm could mine through a foreign-incorporated entity outside the bill's reach.
9. **Sec. 2(3):** "Equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" is undefined, so it's unclear whether removable or temporarily installed equipment counts. Combined with the 5,000 gross ton floor, vessels under that size fall outside the registry and reporting duties even if they mine.
10. **Sec. 2:** "Person" is used in Sec. 3 and 5 but never defined, which affects who is liable and whether individuals, entities, and vessel owners are covered.

**Prohibition (Sec. 3)**

11. **Sec. 3(a):** "In the United States" isn't defined for the territorial sea, the exclusive economic zone, the outer continental shelf, or the extended continental shelf, so coverage of activity in U.S.-claimed waters is uncertain.
12. **Sec. 3(a):** "Engage in" is undefined and doesn't cover financing, insurance, vessel chartering, equipment supply, or purchase, import, or sale of minerals recovered abroad. A company could mine abroad and import the output without violating the bill.
13. **Sec. 3(a):** The bill doesn't reach non-U.S. persons in international waters, foreign-flagged vessels operated by non-U.S. entities, or activity in other countries' exclusive economic zones.
14. **Sec. 3(b):** The exemption covers "mining conducted under an exploration license," but the bill doesn't define "exploration license," doesn't say which licensing regime it means, and doesn't say whether the license must be in good standing. An exploration license authorizes exploration, not commercial recovery, yet the text would cover mining conducted under one.
15. **Sec. 3(b):** The grandfathered activity has no cap on volume, no scope limit, and no bar on renewal, expansion, or transfer of the license.
16. **Sec. 3(b) and Sec. 8:** The exemption is keyed to the enactment date, but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. Licenses issued in that gap are not exempt by the text but also aren't yet covered, which creates an ambiguous window and an incentive to rush licenses.
17. **Sec. 3(c):** "Activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment" is undefined and has no limit on scale, volume, duration, or sale of recovered material. Commercial-scale recovery could be relabeled as assessment.
18. **Sec. 3(c):** The exemption requires no agency approval, no reporting, and no publication of results, so there's no way to tell whether an activity qualifies.

**Registry and reporting (Sec. 4)**

19. **Sec. 4(a):** "Operator" is undefined (owner, charterer, manager, or flag state), so it's unclear who must register a vessel. There is no registration deadline and no required content.
20. **Sec. 4(a) and 5:** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register or report under Sec. 4 carries no penalty, which makes the registry and reporting duties largely unenforceable.
21. **Sec. 4(b):** "Recovery activities" is undefined, and the bill sets no content standard (tonnage, location, depth, discharge, or sediment plumes) and no deadline within each quarter.
22. **Sec. 4(b):** The bill gives NOAA no verification, audit, inspection, or records-retention authority, and it has no penalty for a false certification. The reports therefore depend entirely on operator honesty.
23. **Sec. 4:** The bill doesn't say whether registry information or reports are public or confidential, or how FOIA applies, which affects transparency and litigation.

**Penalties (Sec. 5)**

24. **Sec. 5(a):** The bill doesn't name the agency or process for assessing civil penalties (DOJ or an administrative NOAA process), and it provides no notice, hearing, collection, or judicial review. Without these, penalties may be hard to impose.
25. **Sec. 5(a):** "Violation" and "day" are undefined for continuing activity, and the "not more than" language sets no minimum or aggregate cap. The bill also doesn't say whether the amount is subject to inflation adjustment, which affects its value over the bill's 10-year life.
26. **Sec. 5(a):** The per-day penalty is measured against a company's operating budget, and the bill provides no forfeiture of minerals or vessels, so penalties may be treated as a cost of doing business.
27. **Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8:** "For any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment" conflicts with the 180-day effective date for Sec. 3. Read literally, it either does nothing or suggests a retroactive reach, and it's unclear whether activity during the gap is covered.
28. **Sec. 5:** The bill provides no injunctive relief, vessel detention or seizure, citizen-suit provision, whistleblower protection, or specified limitations period, so enforcement depends on general federal authority.
29. **Sec. 5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined, and the civil standard (strict liability or knowledge-based) is not stated. The bill also doesn't address corporate officer liability or liability of the vessel itself.

**International agreement (Sec. 6)**

30. **Sec. 6:** The Secretary of State must only "seek to negotiate" an agreement within 18 months, with no duty to conclude one, no reporting requirement, and no consequence for failure. "Equivalent" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say whether a future agreement would modify the domestic prohibition or what form it would take (treaty or executive agreement).

**Relationship to existing law (general)**

31. **General:** The bill doesn't say whether it amends, repeals, or preempts the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980, which sets up a NOAA licensing and permitting regime for U.S. entities. That determines what "exploration license" means and creates risk of conflicting regimes and claims by existing license holders. Staff should verify this with CRS or counsel.
32. **General:** The bill is silent on relationships to the International Seabed Authority, UNCLOS-related obligations, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and other federal statutes. Such silence invites preemption and conflict arguments in litigation.

**Duration (Sec. 7)**

33. **Sec. 7(a) and 7(b):** These provisions conflict. Sec. 7(a) says the prohibition stays in effect until a joint resolution is passed, but Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years, so the prohibition can lapse regardless of whether the joint resolution passed. This is the most significant structural problem in the text.
34. **Sec. 7(a):** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say whether the National Academies report must find no serious harm, or what burden applies. The bill also doesn't direct, fund, or set a timeline for the report, so the trigger may never occur or may be unclear.
35. **Sec. 7(a):** The bill doesn't address joint resolution mechanics (expedited procedures or presentment to the President, who can veto). The "finds by joint resolution" phrasing is also unusual, and the bar for lifting the prohibition is high.
36. **Sec. 7(b):** The sunset runs from enactment, not the effective date, so the prohibition has only about 9.5 years in force. The bill has no savings clause for pending violations, penalties, or enforcement actions, so a sunset could end enforcement of violations committed in years nine and ten.

**Effective date (Sec. 8)**

37. **Sec. 8:** The single 180-day effective date covers the whole Act, including the registry, so vessels could operate unregistered for 180 days. Other sections (3(b), 5(a), 6, 7(b)) run from enactment. The bill should set effective dates provision by provision.

**General drafting**

38. **General:** The bill has no severability clause. If a key definition (Sec. 2(1)(A) or 2(2)) is struck down, the regime may fall with it.
39. **General:** The bill gives the Secretary and NOAA no rulemaking authority, no appropriations, no inspection or boarding authority, and no Coast Guard coordination, so the agencies lack the tools to enforce the bill.
40. **General:** The bill has no judicial review or citizen-suit provisions for the Secretary's determinations under Sec. 2(1)(B) or the Sec. 7 findings, which leaves the contested discretionary decisions without a clear review path.

---

**Caveats:** I reviewed only the text you pasted, which is labeled as the October 6 manager's amendment. I haven't checked it against the official congress.gov text or a redline of the amendment, so confirm the version before the markup. The DSHMRA point (item 31) is based on my understanding of that 1980 statute and should be verified against the current U.S. Code. This list addresses drafting and enforceability only and doesn't reflect a position on the bill.
